title: Models, penalties and computation
text:
1 A shared regression structure
After basis expansion, all three model families reduce to penalized regression. For ordinary regression, X contains penalized columns and Z contains unpenalized columns. For scalar-on-function regression, quadrature-weighted curves produce the design \(X_q H\). For function-on-function regression,
\[
Y\approx X_q H\Psi\Theta^\top,
\qquad
\operatorname{vec}(Y)\approx
(\Theta\otimes X_qH)\operatorname{vec}(\Psi),
\]
where \(H\) is \(r\times M\), \(\Theta\) is \(r\times L\), \(X_q\) is \(n\times r\), and \(\Psi\) is \(M\times L\). Columnwise vectorization is consistent with R’s matrix storage convention. The Kronecker design has \(nr\) rows and \(ML\) columns, so increasing both basis sizes can increase computation substantially.


2 Interpret the penalty
Lasso uses coefficientwise absolute values (Tibshirani 1996). Group Lasso uses Euclidean norms of coefficient blocks (Yuan and Lin 2006). Sparse Group Lasso combines the two (Simon et al. 2013). In overlapping-group models, the same coefficient can enter more than one block; this is how a penalty can encode local support of tensor-product B-splines (Jenatton, Audibert, and Bach 2011; Bernardi, Canale, and Stefanucci 2023).
Adaptive penalties set weights using a pilot fit (Zou 2006). Distinguish group weights, coefficient weights inside group norms, and L1 weights: these generally define different penalties. Also distinguish adaptive (statistical weighting) from control$adaptation (ADMM step-size adaptation).
Numerical values of lambda depend on the loss normalization, predictor scaling, grid weights and group weights. A direct comparison with another solver must first align these conventions. The guide deliberately uses each routine’s own path rather than claiming a universal lambda scale.


3 ADMM diagnostics
The package exposes the alternating direction method of multipliers (Boyd et al. 2011; Lin, Li, and Fang 2022). A finite iteration budget does not guarantee convergence. Inspect convergence along the whole path and, if needed, increase control$maxit or inspect the primal and dual residuals. These residuals measure the algorithm’s constraints and stationarity; they are not regression prediction errors.
convergence_table <- data.frame(
 model=c("Lasso","Scalar-on-function","Function-on-function","Inflation"),
 path_points=c(length(fit$lambda),length(scalar_fit$lambda1),
               length(surface_fit$lambda),length(infl_fit$lambda)),
 converged=c(all(fit$convergence==1),all(scalar_fit$convergence==1),
             all(surface_fit$convergence==1),all(infl_fit$convergence==1)))

4 What the selection criteria measure
Training error measures agreement with observed responses. Cross-validation estimates predictive performance under a specified splitting scheme. BIC balances fit and a complexity estimate. These criteria need not choose the same point on a path. Likewise, a fixed-tuning degrees-of-freedom calculation does not automatically include the complexity of choosing the tuning parameter using the same data.
For functional data, split entire independent subjects rather than time points within subjects. For temporally ordered data, preserve time order. For adaptive penalties, recompute pilots and weights using training data only.


5 Reproducibility
All figures and printed numerical results in the guide are generated by its R chunks. Seeds, tuning grids and tolerances appear beside the calls. The build also saves summary tables and the R session information in results/.

title: Function guide
text:
2 Groups and weights
groups=rep(1:4,each=3) defines four disjoint groups. Overlapping groups use list(groups=c(...),Glen=c(...)). group_weights, var_weights and var_weights_L1 have different roles; consult ?lmSP before interchanging them. Group sizes determine the length of group_weights, whereas the number of penalized coefficients determines the length of the variable weights.
For adaptive Lasso use adaptive=TRUE. The linear group examples supply pilot-based group weights explicitly. f2sSP() supports weights_adaptive; its CV companion does not expose that flag. These interfaces are not identical.

title: Function guide
text:
3 Dimensions and domains

Linear paths: tuning values by predictors.
Scalar-on-function paths: tuning values by basis coefficients; function paths replace the basis axis with the observation-grid axis.
Function-on-function coefficient paths: tuning values by predictor basis by response basis.
With smoothing grids, inspect the extra lambda2 dimension before extracting a slice.

The functional tutorials use equally spaced grids on \([0,1]\), cubic B-splines and explicit quadrature weighting. The function-on-function example uses equal predictor and response grid lengths to match the supplied implementation.

title: Inflation: chronological validation
text:
1 An additional validation example
The preceding chapter restores the original model-comparison workflow. This additional example separates training, validation and test periods chronologically, retaining the same dataset and a Lasso fit with fdaSP.
The data are retrieved from the author’s original repository. Here CPIAUCSL is the response and columns 3–74 are predictors, following the original example. This is a chronological regression illustration, not a real-time forecasting experiment: publication lags and data vintages have not been reconstructed.
data_env <- new.env()
load("../data/inflation-Q.RData",envir=data_env)
infl <- data_env$infl.data
y_infl <- as.numeric(infl$CPIAUCSL)
X_infl <- as.matrix(infl[,3:74])
stopifnot(all(is.finite(X_infl)),all(is.finite(y_infl)))
N <- nrow(X_infl)
train <- seq_len(floor(.6*N))
valid <- seq.int(max(train)+1,floor(.8*N))
test <- seq.int(max(valid)+1,N)
data.frame(period=c("Training","Validation","Test"),
           observations=c(length(train),length(valid),length(test)))
##       period observations
## 1   Training           75
## 2 Validation           25
## 3       Test           25


2 Learn scaling on the training period
Centering and scaling use only training observations. We center the response and add its training mean back to predictions. This avoids relying on a package-specific transformation when applying a fitted model to new rows.
xmean <- colMeans(X_infl[train,,drop=FALSE])
xsd <- apply(X_infl[train,,drop=FALSE],2,sd)
keep <- is.finite(xsd) & xsd>0
X_infl <- X_infl[,keep,drop=FALSE]
xmean <- xmean[keep]; xsd <- xsd[keep]
Xs <- sweep(sweep(X_infl,2,xmean,"-"),2,xsd,"/")
ymean <- mean(y_infl[train])
infl_fit <- lmSP(X=Xs[train,,drop=FALSE],y=y_infl[train]-ymean,
                 penalty="LASSO",nlambda=30,lambda.min.ratio=.001,
                 standardize.data=FALSE,control=control)
check_path(infl_fit)
valid_predictions <- Xs[valid,,drop=FALSE] %*% t(infl_fit$sp.coef.path)+ymean
validation_mse <- colMeans((valid_predictions-y_infl[valid])^2)
i_infl <- which.min(validation_mse)
test_predictions <- drop(Xs[test,,drop=FALSE] %*% infl_fit$sp.coef.path[i_infl,])+ymean
inflation_results <- data.frame(lambda=infl_fit$lambda[i_infl],
 validation_MSE=min(validation_mse),test_MSE=mean((y_infl[test]-test_predictions)^2),
 training_mean_baseline_MSE=mean((y_infl[test]-ymean)^2))
inflation_results
##       lambda validation_MSE    test_MSE training_mean_baseline_MSE
## 1 0.00965022   0.0004732347 0.001037905                0.001037931
ggplot(data.frame(lambda=infl_fit$lambda,mse=validation_mse),aes(lambda,mse)) +
 geom_line(colour="#9e1b32") + geom_vline(xintercept=infl_fit$lambda[i_infl],linetype=2) +
 scale_x_log10() + labs(x=expression(lambda),y="Chronological validation MSE")



Validation error over the inflation regression path. The test period is not used to choose lambda.


infl_plot <- data.frame(observation=rep(test,2),value=c(y_infl[test],test_predictions),
                        series=rep(c("Observed","Predicted"),each=length(test)))
ggplot(infl_plot,aes(observation,value,colour=series)) + geom_line() + geom_point(size=1.2) +
 labs(x="Observation index",y="Inflation",colour=NULL)



Observed inflation and predictions over the held-out final period; the horizontal axis retains the data’s row order.


The result is one held-out comparison, not evidence of universal superiority. For a forecasting study, use predictors available at each forecast origin and rolling or expanding training windows. The original comparisons with other packages are executed and discussed in the preceding chapter.

title: Function-on-function regression
text:
1 A locally sparse coefficient surface
A functional response depends on a functional predictor through a surface:
\[
y_i(s)=\int_0^1 x_i(t)\psi(t,s)\,\mathrm dt+\varepsilon_i(s),
\qquad
\psi(t,s)=\boldsymbol\varphi(t)^\top\boldsymbol\Psi\boldsymbol\theta(s).
\]
The \(M\times L\) coefficient matrix connects predictor-domain and response-domain basis functions. Locally sparse function-on-function regression uses an overlapping-group penalty adapted to this tensor-product basis (Bernardi, Canale, and Stefanucci 2023). The example uses \(M=8\), \(L=5\) and a surface supported on only part of the domain.
We retain the predictor curves and quadrature convention from the previous chapter. In this version of f2fSP(), both basis grids are constructed from the number of columns of mX; use the same grid length for predictor and response in this workflow.
set.seed(301)
Theta <- splines::bs(t,df=5,intercept=TRUE)
Psi_true <- matrix(0,8,5)
Psi_true[3:4,2:3] <- 2
surface_true <- H %*% Psi_true %*% t(Theta)
Y_curves <- X_quad %*% surface_true +
  matrix(rnorm(n_fun*length(t),sd=.04),n_fun,length(t))


2 Estimate the surface and choose the tuning parameter
surface_fit <- f2fSP(mY=Y_curves,mX=X_quad,M=8,L=5,
                     nlambda=20,lambda.min.ratio=.001,
                     standardize.data=FALSE,control=control)
check_path(surface_fit)
set.seed(302)
surface_cv <- f2fSP_cv(mY=Y_curves,mX=X_quad,M=8,L=5,
                       lambda=surface_fit$lambda,cv.fold=5,
                       standardize.data=FALSE,control=control)
i_surface <- which.min(abs(surface_fit$lambda-surface_cv$lambda.min))
Psi_est <- surface_fit$sp.coef.path[i_surface,,]
surface_est <- H %*% Psi_est %*% t(Theta)
stopifnot(max(abs(surface_est-surface_fit$sp.fun.path[i_surface,,]))<1e-8)
We reconstruct the selected surface explicitly from sp.coef.path, whose first dimension indexes the tuning parameter. This also makes the predictor and response axes unambiguous.
surface_plot <- rbind(
  transform(expand.grid(t=t,s=t),value=as.vector(surface_true),panel="Truth"),
  transform(expand.grid(t=t,s=t),value=as.vector(surface_est),panel="CV estimate"))
ggplot(surface_plot,aes(t,s,fill=value)) + geom_raster() + coord_equal() +
  facet_wrap(~panel) + scale_fill_gradient2(low="#2166ac",mid="white",high="#b2182b") +
  labs(x="Predictor domain t",y="Response domain s",fill=expression(psi(t,s)))



True and estimated coefficient surfaces on a common colour scale. Horizontal coordinates index the predictor domain; vertical coordinates index the response domain.




3 Examine the path and predict curves
surface_path_matrix <- matrix(surface_fit$sp.coef.path,
                               nrow=length(surface_fit$lambda))
ggplot(path_data(surface_path_matrix,surface_fit$lambda),
       aes(lambda,coefficient,group=term)) + geom_line(colour="#9e1b32",alpha=.6) +
  scale_x_log10() + labs(x=expression(lambda),y="Tensor-product coefficient")



Tensor-product coefficient paths; the first array dimension indexes the regularization parameter.


set.seed(303)
Ynew <- Xnew_quad %*% surface_true +
  matrix(rnorm(nrow(Xnew_quad)*length(t),sd=.04),nrow(Xnew_quad),length(t))
Ypred <- Xnew_quad %*% surface_est
subject <- 1
curve_prediction <- data.frame(s=rep(t,2),value=c(Ynew[subject,],Ypred[subject,]),
                                curve=rep(c("Observed","Predicted"),each=length(t)))
mean((Ynew-Ypred)^2)
## [1] 0.001580285
ggplot(curve_prediction,aes(s,value,colour=curve)) + geom_line(linewidth=.8) +
  labs(x="Response domain",y="Response",colour=NULL)



Observed and predicted response for a held-out subject.


Prediction error and recovery of the coefficient surface answer different questions. A correlated functional design can predict well without uniquely recovering every feature of a surface. The test subjects above are separate from the subjects used for fitting and CV. f2fSP() does not return a dof component in the supplied version; this guide does not substitute a count of nonzero basis coefficients for a functional degrees-of-freedom formula.








References

Bernardi, Mauro, Antonio Canale, and Marco Stefanucci. 2023. “Locally Sparse Function-on-Function Regression.” Journal of Computational and Graphical Statistics 32 (3): 985–99. https://doi.org/10.1080/10618600.2022.2130926.

title: Inflation: the complete model-comparison workflow
text:
1 The data and the scope of the comparison
This chapter develops the inflation analysis in the original repository: correlations, ordinary least squares, Lasso and Elastic Net, best-subset selection, adaptive penalties, Bayesian model averaging, and the fdaSP implementation. The one-lag specification uses 18 macroeconomic predictors; the four-lag specification uses all 72 predictor columns.
These are full-sample model-comparison exercises. Random-fold cross-validation is retained from the original workflow and must not be interpreted as a real-time forecasting assessment. The separate chronological analysis later in this guide uses training, validation and test periods.
The repository relates the data to the inflation application discussed by Bernardi et al. (2024). We retain the supplied transformations rather than reconstructing them from raw economic series. Inspecting the supplied file reveals 125 observations, from July 1991 to July 2022. The older prose mentioned 2023-Q4, but that endpoint is not present in this data file. The response used below is CPIAUCSL; CPILFESL, mentioned in the old introduction, is not a column in this version of the dataset.
library(fdaSP)
library(ggplot2)
stopifnot(all(vapply(c("glmnet","leaps","BMS","corrplot"),
                    requireNamespace,logical(1),quietly=TRUE)))
original_data <- new.env()
load("../data/inflation-Q.RData",envir=original_data)
inflation <- original_data$infl.data
y_original <- as.numeric(inflation$CPIAUCSL)
lag1_names <- grep("_l1$",names(inflation),value=TRUE)
all_lag_names <- grep("_l[1-4]$",names(inflation),value=TRUE)
X1 <- as.matrix(inflation[,lag1_names])
X4 <- as.matrix(inflation[,all_lag_names])
stopifnot(ncol(X1)==18L,ncol(X4)==72L,
          all(is.finite(X4)),all(is.finite(y_original)))
data.frame(observations=nrow(inflation),first=min(inflation$DATE),
           last=max(inflation$DATE),one_lag=ncol(X1),four_lags=ncol(X4))
##   observations   first    last one_lag four_lags
## 1          125 1991-07 2022-07      18        72
All results and figures below are regenerated by the guide. The packages glmnet, leaps, BMS and corrplot are additional dependencies of this application, not additional dependencies imposed on fdaSP itself.


2 Preliminary correlations and one-lag OLS
As in the original example, the correlation plot uses inflation and the first lag of each macroeconomic indicator. Standardization does not change these correlations. Ellipses reveal both their sign and strength.
X1_scaled <- scale(X1)
y_original_scaled <- drop(scale(y_original))
correlation_data <- cbind(INFL=y_original_scaled,X1_scaled)
correlation_matrix <- cor(correlation_data)
corrplot::corrplot(correlation_matrix,order="AOE",method="ellipse",
                   type="upper",tl.cex=.65,tl.col="#333333",mar=c(0,0,1,0))



Inflation and the 18 first-lag macroeconomic predictors. Variables are ordered by the angular order of eigenvectors (AOE), as in the original analysis.


The OLS specification includes an intercept and all 18 first-lag regressors. The summary reproduces the coefficient estimates and conventional standard errors of the original workflow. These standard errors do not correct for serial dependence or subsequent model selection.

3 Lasso and Elastic Net with glmnet
glmnet computes penalized paths using coordinate descent (Friedman, Hastie, and Tibshirani 2010). We retain the Lasso path and the Elastic Net comparison with mixing parameter \(\alpha=0.5\), and also show Lasso CV explicitly. Both CV fits use the same ten folds. Each refit uses the same predictor set and mixing parameter as the CV fit that selected its tuning parameter.
set.seed(42)
folds1 <- sample(rep(seq_len(10),length.out=length(y_original)))
lasso1 <- glmnet::glmnet(X1,y_original,alpha=1,standardize=TRUE,nlambda=100)
cv_lasso1 <- glmnet::cv.glmnet(X1,y_original,alpha=1,standardize=TRUE,
                              nlambda=100,foldid=folds1)
cv_enet1 <- glmnet::cv.glmnet(X1,y_original,alpha=.5,standardize=TRUE,
                             nlambda=100,foldid=folds1)
enet1_selected <- glmnet::glmnet(X1,y_original,alpha=.5,standardize=TRUE,
                                 lambda=cv_enet1$lambda.min)
For plotting, we keep the coefficient paths on their original response scale and display \(\lambda\) on a logarithmic axis. The helper below retains predictor names, which are useful when inspecting selected variables.
glmnet_path_data <- function(object,label) {
  b <- as.matrix(object$beta)
  data.frame(lambda=rep(object$lambda,each=nrow(b)),
             coefficient=as.vector(b),
             term=rep(rownames(b),times=ncol(b)),method=label)
}
glmnet_cv_data <- function(object,label) {
  data.frame(lambda=object$lambda,mse=object$cvm,se=object$cvsd,method=label)
}
selected_coefficients <- function(object,rule,label) {
  b <- as.matrix(coef(object,s=rule))
  keep <- b[,1]!=0
  data.frame(method=label,rule=rule,term=rownames(b)[keep],
             coefficient=as.numeric(b[keep,1]),row.names=NULL)
}
ggplot(glmnet_path_data(lasso1,"Lasso"),aes(lambda,coefficient,group=term)) +
  geom_line(colour="#9e1b32",alpha=.65) + scale_x_log10() +
  labs(x=expression(lambda),y="Coefficient")



One-lag Lasso coefficient paths from glmnet; each line represents one macroeconomic regressor.


one_cv <- rbind(glmnet_cv_data(cv_lasso1,"Lasso"),
                 glmnet_cv_data(cv_enet1,"Elastic Net"))
one_cv_choices <- data.frame(method=c("Lasso","Elastic Net"),
                              lambda=c(cv_lasso1$lambda.min,cv_enet1$lambda.min))
ggplot(one_cv,aes(lambda,mse)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin=mse-se,ymax=mse+se),fill="#9e1b32",alpha=.15) +
  geom_line(colour="#9e1b32") +
  geom_vline(data=one_cv_choices,aes(xintercept=lambda),linetype=2) +

retained_model_table <- function(fit, n=8L) {
  tab <- BMS::topmodels.bma(fit)
  weights <- tab["PMP (Exact)", ]
  stopifnot(all(is.finite(weights)), all(weights >= 0), sum(weights) > 0)
  weights <- weights / sum(weights)
  out <- rbind(tab[fit$reg.names, , drop=FALSE],
               "Posterior weight conditional on retained models"=weights)
  out[, seq_len(min(n,ncol(out))), drop=FALSE]

9 What was clarified during restoration
All substantive analyses in the original R Markdown are represented above. The main corrections are consistent use of one- versus four-lag designs, matching \(\alpha\) between CV and refitting, explicit lambda.min versus lambda.1se, and the distinction between the two packages’ uncertainty bands. The supplied data determine the reported date range. Ridge-pilot adaptive Lasso is shown in addition to the original OLS-pilot fit, and the BMS retained model count is aligned with the original comment about 100 models.
The old “Real estate dataset” heading had no data, code or results beneath it. No real-estate application is invented here. The original source remains unchanged in archive/original-README.Rmd; the chronological analysis in the next chapter is an addition to this restored workflow.

title: Linear regression and regularization paths
text:
1 Prepare the session
Run the examples in chapter order, or use the downloadable R script. These helpers define solver tolerances, reshape path matrices for plotting, and check convergence. Subsequent chapters reuse them.
library(fdaSP)
library(ggplot2)
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size=12)+theme(legend.position="bottom"))
ctl <- list(maxit=3000, abstol=1e-6, reltol=1e-6, print.out=FALSE)
path_data <- function(path, lambda) {
  path <- as.matrix(path)
  stopifnot(nrow(path)==length(lambda))
  data.frame(lambda=rep(lambda,ncol(path)), coefficient=as.vector(path),
             term=factor(rep(seq_len(ncol(path)),each=nrow(path))))
}
check_path <- function(fit) {
  stopifnot(all(is.finite(fit$sp.coef.path)), all(fit$convergence==1))
}


2 Start with a sparse signal
lmSP() fits a path; lmSP_cv() selects a tuning parameter by cross-validation. The same interface covers Lasso, Group Lasso, sparse Group Lasso and their overlapping-group counterparts. We begin with 12 predictors and three nonzero coefficients, so that the fitted path can be compared with a known signal.
set.seed(101)
n <- 100
p <- 12
X <- matrix(rnorm(n*p), n, p)
beta <- c(2,-1,1,rep(0,p-3))
y <- drop(X %*% beta) + rnorm(n)
lambda <- 10^seq(0.7,-2,length.out=30)
control <- ctl
The grid is decreasing and equally spaced on a logarithmic scale. We set standardize.data=FALSE explicitly: the simulated predictors already have comparable scales, and predictions below then use the original design directly. On real data, learn centering and scaling from the training sample and reuse them for validation and prediction. An unpenalized intercept can be requested with intercept=TRUE; other unpenalized covariates can be supplied through Z.
fit <- lmSP(X=X, y=y, penalty="LASSO", lambda=lambda,
            standardize.data=FALSE, intercept=FALSE, control=control)
check_path(fit)
dim(fit$sp.coef.path)
## [1] 30 12
Each row of sp.coef.path corresponds to a value of lambda; each column corresponds to a predictor. This orientation matters when calculating predictions.
ggplot(path_data(fit$sp.coef.path,fit$lambda),
       aes(lambda,coefficient,colour=term)) + geom_line(linewidth=.65) +
  scale_x_log10() + labs(x=expression(lambda),y="Coefficient",colour="Predictor")



Lasso coefficient paths. The horizontal axis is logarithmic; each line is one predictor.




3 Select a model and predict
The path object’s lambda.min minimizes training MSE. It is not the cross-validation choice. Use the CV result to select a row of the path, or refit at the selected value. The example splits observations into folds, appropriate for independent sampling; time-series examples need a different split.
set.seed(102)
cv <- lmSP_cv(X=X, y=y, penalty="LASSO", lambda=fit$lambda,
              cv.fold=5, standardize.data=FALSE, control=control)
i_cv <- which.min(abs(fit$lambda-cv$lambda.min))
beta_cv <- as.numeric(fit$sp.coef.path[i_cv,])
Xnew <- matrix(rnorm(40*p),40,p)
ynew <- drop(Xnew %*% beta) + rnorm(40)
pred <- drop(Xnew %*% beta_cv)
data.frame(lambda=cv$lambda.min, test_MSE=mean((ynew-pred)^2))
##     lambda test_MSE
## 1 0.130991 1.042146
ggplot(data.frame(lambda=cv$lambda,mse=as.numeric(cv$mse)),aes(lambda,mse)) +
  geom_line(colour="#9e1b32") + geom_point(size=1.5) +
  geom_vline(xintercept=cv$lambda.min,linetype=2) + scale_x_log10() +
  labs(x=expression(lambda),y="Cross-validated MSE")



Cross-validated prediction error and the selected tuning parameter.




4 Compare the five penalty families
Disjoint groups are encoded by a membership vector. For overlapping groups, use a list whose groups element concatenates the member indices and whose Glen element records the length of each group. A predictor may appear more than once in the concatenated vector.
groups <- rep(1:4,each=3)
overlap <- list(groups=c(1:4,4:7,7:10,10:12),Glen=c(4,4,4,3))
family_args <- list(
  LASSO=list(),
  GLASSO=list(groups=groups),
  spGLASSO=list(groups=groups,alpha=.5),
  OVGLASSO=list(groups=overlap),
  spOVGLASSO=list(groups=overlap,alpha=.5))
fits <- lapply(names(family_args),function(method) {
  do.call(lmSP,c(list(X=X,y=y,penalty=method,lambda=lambda,
                     standardize.data=FALSE,control=control),family_args[[method]]))
})
names(fits) <- names(family_args)
invisible(lapply(fits,check_path))
paths <- do.call(rbind,lapply(names(fits),function(method) {
  d <- path_data(fits[[method]]$sp.coef.path,fits[[method]]$lambda)
  d$method <- method
  d
}))
ggplot(paths,aes(lambda,coefficient,group=term,colour=term)) +
  geom_line(linewidth=.55) + scale_x_log10() + facet_wrap(~method,ncol=2) +
  labs(x=expression(lambda),y="Coefficient") + theme(legend.position="none")



Coefficient paths under five penalties, using the same response and tuning grid. Equal numerical tuning parameters do not imply equal penalty strength across methods.


Group Lasso selects groups, whereas sparse Group Lasso also allows within-group sparsity (Yuan and Lin 2006; Simon et al. 2013). Overlapping groups express shared structure; the penalty acts on repeated group memberships rather than on a partition (Jenatton, Audibert, and Bach 2011).


5 Adaptive penalties
For Lasso, adaptive=TRUE requests the package’s adaptive scheme. For group penalties, the example below supplies explicit pilot-based group weights. These are distinct from var_weights, which act on individual coefficients. In the supplied version, the lmSP() group branches do not forward weights_adaptive to their solvers, so explicit weights make the intended penalty unambiguous.
adaptive_lasso <- lmSP(X=X,y=y,penalty="LASSO",adaptive=TRUE,
                       lambda=lambda,standardize.data=FALSE,control=control)
## Warning in linreg_ADMM_LASSO(X = X, Z = Z, y = y, var_weights = var_weights, : * lmSP : adaptive Lasso is running!
pilot <- drop(qr.solve(X,y))
pilot_norms <- vapply(split(pilot,groups),function(b) sqrt(sum(b^2)),numeric(1))
group_weights <- 1/pmax(pilot_norms,1e-4)
adaptive_group <- lmSP(X=X,y=y,penalty="GLASSO",groups=groups,
                       group_weights=group_weights,lambda=lambda,
                       standardize.data=FALSE,control=control)
check_path(adaptive_lasso)
check_path(adaptive_group)
The floor 1e-4 is an explicit numerical choice for this example, not an identity for inverse weights at zero. Pilot weights are data dependent (Zou 2006). When evaluating an adaptive procedure by CV, recompute its pilot and weights inside each training fold; supplying full-sample weights to an ordinary CV call does not do this automatically.


6 Inspect degrees of freedom along the path
The tested version returns dof and bic for Lasso and Group Lasso. The sparse-group and overlapping-group fits do not currently return these components. The plot includes only fits for which a DoF vector is actually returned; it does not replace missing values by a count of nonzero coefficients. For the explicit pilot-weighted Group Lasso example above, the group solver reports a fixed-weight contribution, not the full correction for data-dependent weights.
dof_methods <- names(fits)[vapply(fits,function(z) !is.null(z$dof),logical(1))]
df_paths <- do.call(rbind,lapply(dof_methods,function(method) {
  z <- fits[[method]]
  stopifnot(length(z$dof)==length(z$lambda))
  data.frame(lambda=z$lambda,dof=as.numeric(z$dof),method=method)
}))
ggplot(df_paths,aes(lambda,dof,colour=method)) + geom_line(linewidth=.7) +
  scale_x_log10() + labs(x=expression(lambda),y="Estimated degrees of freedom",colour=NULL)



Degrees-of-freedom estimates returned by fdaSP along the available fitted paths.










References

Jenatton, Rodolphe, Jean-Yves Audibert, and Francis Bach. 2011. “Structured Variable Selection with Sparsity-Inducing Norms.” J. Mach. Learn. Res. 12: 2777–2824.


Simon, Noah, Jerome Friedman, Trevor Hastie, and Robert Tibshirani. 2013. “A Sparse-Group Lasso.” J. Comput. Graph. Statist. 22 (2): 231–45. https://doi.org/10.1080/10618600.2012.681250.


Yuan, Ming, and Yi Lin. 2006. “Model Selection and Estimation in Regression with Grouped Variables.” Journal of the Royal Statistical Society: Series B (Statistical Methodology) 68 (1): 49–67.


Zou, Hui. 2006. “The Adaptive Lasso and Its Oracle Properties.” J. Amer. Statist. Assoc. 101 (476): 1418–29. https://doi.org/10.1198/016214506000000735.

title: Scalar-on-function regression
text:
1 From predictor curves to a coefficient curve
For subject \(i\), the model relates a scalar response to a predictor curve:
\[
y_i=\int_0^1 x_i(t)\psi(t)\,\mathrm dt+\varepsilon_i,
\qquad \psi(t)=\boldsymbol\varphi(t)^\top\boldsymbol\psi.
\]
f2sSP() represents the coefficient function with B-splines and imposes an overlapping-group penalty on the basis coefficients. Local support of the basis makes it possible to estimate regions where the coefficient function is zero. Here the curve has eight basis coefficients, of which three are nonzero.
Grid convention. The current implementation forms mX %*% H, where H contains basis values, without adding quadrature weights. We therefore multiply the sampled predictor curves by trapezoidal weights before fitting. The same weighted matrix is used for simulation and prediction. This makes the matrix product approximate the displayed integral rather than an unscaled sum.
set.seed(201)
n_fun <- 80
t <- seq(0,1,length.out=41)
H <- splines::bs(t,df=8,intercept=TRUE)
curve_scores <- matrix(rnorm(n_fun*8),n_fun,8)
X_curves <- curve_scores %*% t(H)
qweight <- c(.5,rep(1,length(t)-2),.5)*diff(t)[1]
X_quad <- sweep(X_curves,2,qweight,"*")
psi_true <- drop(H %*% c(0,0,2,2,-1,0,0,0))
y_fun <- drop(X_quad %*% psi_true) + rnorm(n_fun,sd=.08)
curves <- data.frame(t=rep(t,6),x=as.vector(t(X_curves[1:6,])),
                     subject=factor(rep(1:6,each=length(t))))
ggplot(curves,aes(t,x,colour=subject)) + geom_line() +
  labs(x="Domain",y="Predictor value",colour="Subject")



Six predictor curves before quadrature weighting.




2 Fit and select the curve
We use cubic B-splines (splOrd=4) on the package’s equally spaced grid on \([0,1]\). The input rows represent subjects, not time points. The package’s CV routine splits subjects; it does not split individual points from a curve.
scalar_fit <- f2sSP(vY=y_fun,mX=X_quad,M=8,splOrd=4,
                    nlambda1=25,lambda1.min.ratio=.001,
                    standardize.data=FALSE,control=control)
check_path(scalar_fit)
set.seed(202)
scalar_cv <- f2sSP_cv(vY=y_fun,mX=X_quad,M=8,splOrd=4,
                      lambda1=scalar_fit$lambda1,cv.fold=5,
                      standardize.data=FALSE,control=control)
i_scalar <- which.min(abs(scalar_fit$lambda1-scalar_cv$lambda1.min.mse))
psi_est <- drop(H %*% scalar_fit$sp.coef.path[i_scalar,])
stopifnot(max(abs(psi_est-scalar_fit$sp.fun.path[i_scalar,]))<1e-8)
curve_comparison <- data.frame(t=rep(t,2),value=c(psi_true,psi_est),
                               curve=rep(c("Truth","CV estimate"),each=length(t)))
ggplot(curve_comparison,aes(t,value,colour=curve)) + geom_line(linewidth=.85) +
  scale_colour_manual(values=c("CV estimate"="#9e1b32","Truth"="#334e68")) +
  labs(x="Domain",y=expression(psi(t)),colour=NULL)



True coefficient curve and the estimate selected by subject-level cross-validation.




3 Follow the path and predict new responses
sp.coef.path stores basis coefficients, while sp.fun.path stores the corresponding function values. Examining both separates coefficient shrinkage from changes in the shape of the regression function.
ggplot(path_data(scalar_fit$sp.coef.path,scalar_fit$lambda1),
       aes(lambda,coefficient,colour=term)) + geom_line() + scale_x_log10() +
  labs(x=expression(lambda[1]),y="Basis coefficient",colour="Basis")



Basis-coefficient paths for the scalar-on-function model.


set.seed(203)
Xnew_curves <- matrix(rnorm(30*8),30,8) %*% t(H)
Xnew_quad <- sweep(Xnew_curves,2,qweight,"*")
ynew_fun <- drop(Xnew_quad %*% psi_true)+rnorm(30,sd=.08)
pred_fun <- drop(Xnew_quad %*% psi_est)
data.frame(test_MSE=mean((ynew_fun-pred_fun)^2),
           curve_integrated_squared_error=sum(qweight*(psi_est-psi_true)^2))
##      test_MSE curve_integrated_squared_error
## 1 0.007965336                    0.006860105


4 Degrees of freedom, BIC and smoothing
lambda1.min.bic selects the BIC minimum; lambda1.min.mse selects the training-MSE minimum. Neither name denotes the CV optimum. The implementation computes BIC as \(n\log(\mathrm{MSE})+\log(n)\widehat{\mathrm{df}}\); plot both components to understand the trade-off. Selecting a tuning parameter on the same data introduces a further layer of model selection.
scalar_diagnostics <- data.frame(lambda=rep(scalar_fit$lambda1,3),
 value=c(scalar_fit$mse,scalar_fit$bic,scalar_fit$dof),
 measure=rep(c("Training MSE","BIC","Degrees of freedom"),each=length(scalar_fit$lambda1)))
ggplot(scalar_diagnostics,aes(lambda,value)) + geom_line(colour="#9e1b32") +
 scale_x_log10() + facet_wrap(~measure,scales="free_y",ncol=1) +
 labs(x=expression(lambda[1]),y=NULL)



Training error, BIC and the returned degrees-of-freedom estimate across the scalar-on-function path.


The optional lambda2 controls a finite-difference roughness penalty. With several smoothing values, output dimensions gain an additional grid axis. Always inspect dim() before selecting a slice.
smooth_fit <- f2sSP(vY=y_fun,mX=X_quad,M=8,lambda1=scalar_fit$lambda1,
                    lambda2=c(.001,.01),diff_order=2,
                    standardize.data=FALSE,control=control)
check_path(smooth_fit)
dim(smooth_fit$sp.coef.path)
## [1] 25  2  8
This example uses fixed weights. f2sSP() also offers weights_adaptive=TRUE; its CV companion has a different signature, so adaptive validation should be constructed explicitly with training-fold pilots.
